catalog_quote: 4.2.1.1 TONES heavy ... creaky ... low ... stop ... weak ... [p. 97] 4.2.2 PHONEME DESCRIPTION All sounds are realised as in SB except as set out below: Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones, but there is a difference in clause intonation matched by differences in syllable tone. The study of intonation is not within the scope of these notes, but an obvious feature is the relatively low pitch, compared with SB, of TV syllables in the stop tone. [p. 98] ... 4.2.3.1 TONES These are as in SB. [p. 98] ... 4.3.2.2 WEAKENING Weakening occurs in TV in the same way, and with the same voicing pattern, as in SB. ... Two differences emerged: one is that TV ... 'two', unlike its SB counterpart ..., does not weaken in compounds. ... The other is that a number of words with weak syllables in SB have counterparts in TV with no matching syllable at all. [p. 107]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (+, extracted text, PL A-83 2015 online edition, author John Okell) opened and read. All three locators check out against the running page headers in the text: (1) §4.2.1.1 TONES on p. 97 (the text) lists exactly five entries heavy / creaky / low / stop / weak; the compiler quote substitutes placeholder marks /˘/ for the tone diacritics because the scanned renders them as "1t.1", "1+1", "1+'1", "Igl" — that is the only difference, and it is cosmetic. (2) §4.2.2 PHONEME DESCRIPTION on p. 98 (lines 4701-4705): "All sounds are realised as in SB except as set out below: Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones, but there is a difference in clause intonation matched by differences in syll…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tavoyan is described as a tone language with the same five-way syllable-tone system as Standard Burmese (heavy, creaky, low, stop, plus 'weak' = reduced schwa syllables); Okell says nothing about word stress and explicitly puts intonation outside the scope of the notes. Prominence is handled, as in Burmese, by the full-vs-weak (major/minor) syllable contrast rather than by a stated stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Two differences in weakening from Standard Burmese (p. 107): TV /hne/ 'two' does not weaken in compounds, and a number of words with weak syllables in SB have Tavoyan counterparts with no matching syllable at all (e.g. SB /səbá/ 'paddy' = TV /bá/).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable tone and word-internal weakening (compounds, numeral+classifier); intonation of clauses noted only as different from SB and out of scope. Ono 1971 (p. 114) independently gives a three-way tone statement for Tavoy with no stress remark.
new_statements.identity_note: Okell 1995 describes the Tavoyan (TV) of Tavoy/Dawei town (informant U Ca Min, recordings c. 1960s-70s) = tavo1242. Ono 1971 covers the same Tavoy dialect plus Mergui. Kato & Khin Pale 2012 describes Myeik (Beik), which they treat as a separate 'Myeik group' from the 'Dawei group' (not tavo1242 proper; Glottolog has no separate code visible for Myeik in the Tavoyan record). Glottolog notes alt. name 'Myanmar'. No sub-dialect issue for the Okell material.

tone_statements.quote: 3.3. 声調 本稿ではパロー方言を記述するにあたり，以下の声調素を用いる。尚，上昇の声調では，付随的な特徴として母音に咽喉の緊張が認められる。 表 4 声調素 声調素の名称 中平 高平 上昇 表記 /ᴹ/ /ᴴ/ /ᴿ/ 代表的なピッチ [33] [55] [13] 末子音 /ʔ/ を伴う促音節には示差的な声調が現れず，常に低いピッチ [11] で発音される。ビルマ語の研究者によってはこの促音節のピッチパターンを独立した声調素として見なす場合がある。パロー方言でこれを別個の声調素と見なすべきかどうかについては更に詳細な分析が必要なので，本稿では暫定的に 3 種類の声調素を用いて考察を進めたい。
tone_statements.translation: 3.3 Tones. In describing the Palaw dialect this paper uses the following tonemes. In the rising tone, laryngeal tension on the vowel is observed as an accompanying feature. Table 4, Tonemes: name mid-level / high-level / rising; notation /M/ /H/ /R/; representative pitch [33] [55] [13]. Checked syllables with final /ʔ/ show no distinctive tone and are always pronounced at low pitch [11]. Some scholars of Burmese regard the pitch pattern of these checked syllables as an independent toneme. Whether it should be treated as a separate toneme in the Palaw dialect requires more detailed analysis, so this paper provisionally proceeds with three tonemes.
tone_statements.locator: p. 167, §3.3 声調 (Table 4 声調素); tone correspondences §4.3, p. 171
tone_statements.summary: Palaw sub-dialect: 3 tonemes M [33], H [55], R [13]+laryngeal tension (= SB low, high, creaky); checked /ʔ/ syllables non-contrastive low [11]; toneless reduced /ă/ syllables; syllable TBU; minor H-M sandhi.

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko & Khin Pale. 2012. The Myeik (Beik) dialect of Burmese: Sounds, conversational texts, and basic vocabulary. Journal of Asian and African Studies (アジア・アフリカ言語文化研究) 83: 117-160. Tokyo: ILCAA, TUFS.
sources.note: Describes the neighbouring Myeik (Beik) dialect, which the authors place in a 'Myeik group' distinct from the 'Dawei group' (pp. 118-119). Tone system described (rising tone with pharyngealization, phonation-prominent tone system); nothing on stress. Useful for its literature list on the Dawei dialect: Taylor 1921, Pe Maung Tin 1933, Bernot 1965, Ono 1971, Khin Pale 1979, Okell 1995 (p. 118).

sources.note: Tavoy dialect pp. 101-114, Mergui pp. 114-121. Only tone: p. 114 item (5) 'タボイ方言の声調体系は，標準語同様（i）低平型，（ii）緊喉母音に伴なう高短型，（iii）高平型の三種である。' [The tone system of the Tavoy dialect, like the standard language, has three types: (i) low level, (ii) high-short with creaky vowel, (iii) high level]. No mention of stress/accent (アクセント/強勢) for Tavoy; 'neutral tone' (無声調, schwa syllables) discussed only for Mergui.

sources.note: §3 phonology gives an explicit tone analysis for Palaw: three tonemes mid-level /M/ [33], high-level /H/ [55], rising /R/ [13] with accompanying laryngeal tension; checked syllables in final /ʔ/ carry no distinctive tone and are always low [11] with more audible creak than in Yangon/Mandalay; a sandhi H+M -> [55 53] in one speaker (possibly idiosyncratic); toneless 'light' syllables with /ă/; §4.3 (p. 171) shows Palaw M, H, R correspond to Yangon Burmese low, high and creaky tones respectively. Every vocabulary item is tone-marked.
